results.content: # Adversary-Based Threat Modeling Adversary-based threat modeling is designed to help security teams make valuable defensive decisions, and defend them with evidence. Most threat models start with an inventory of critical assets or an attack surface map, but this is not how adversaries see our organization. The most important part of this threat model is understanding our adversaries. Follow this process for all our adversaries and their playbooks and tally up the results weighed by how likely each adversary is to target you, and and now you have a prioritized list of effective defenses for our organization. results.title: How Assumptions Can Kill Your Software Product
results.content: Assumption mapping changed how I approach software development, and it can transform your product decisions, too. In my years building software products, I’ve watched teams pour months into features that users ignore, technologies that break, and business models that fail. The problem is that we build on assumptions we never test. Assumption mapping provides a systematic approach to identify what you believe, test what matters, and build with confidence rather than hope. When you map your assumptions before you code, you can test the risky ones early and avoid building products that nobody wants. Software teams need to validate four types of product risk: value, usability, feasibility, and viability. Different types of assumptions require different validation approaches, and you don’t always need to build working software to test them. ### **Building Assumption Mapping Into Your Development Process**. When you make assumptions explicit and test the important ones early, you build better products and waste less time on features that don’t matter.

results.title: How do model assumptions impact the interpretation of results in machine learning? - Data Science Stack Exchange
results.content: # How do model assumptions impact the interpretation of results in machine learning? When training a machine learning model, we often focus on performance metrics and generalization. However, each type of model comes with implicit assumptions about the data structure. The question of how implicit (and explicit) model assumptions influence predictive performance lies at the heart of applied machine learning. Every model class encodes inductive biases: structural assumptions about how inputs relate to outputs. Predictive performance emerges not just from model capacity, but from the *alignment* between the model’s assumptions and the data’s underlying patterns. More robust alternatives involve assessing model stability under resampling schemes (eg., cross-validation) with different seeds) or evaluating performance across subgroups, time periods, or data sources. Transforming the data to better match model assumptions can often improve performance. ### Meta-Learning and Structured Model Selection. The essence of predictive machine learning lies not in selecting the “best” model, but in aligning model structure with data geometry.
